new_statements.quote: 2. Dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than syllable pitch, but most languages have some lexical tone doublets, e.g. KATCHA: nyá hill, nyà wind, 'ofo to vomit, 'ôfò mound, (stress here denoted by ' preceding stressed syllable). Lexical stress-tone doublets also occur, e.g. KRONGO: 'kûrùgù husks, ku'rûgù kidneys. Stress may also cause the disappearance of vowels, as in KAMDANG: ta-m'dədək, pl. ka-m'dədək smith, (c.f. MIRI ta-mədədək / ka-mədədək) KATCHA: 'balade or 'balde bag, nefo, pl. nan'fone giraffe, KRONGO: fa tree, aka ki'da f[a] climb the tree.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stevenson describes the Kadugli-Krongo (Kadu) languages, illustrated chiefly from Katcha, as stress-dominant: dynamic stress matters more than syllable pitch, though Katcha has a few lexical tone minimal pairs; stress position can itself be lexically contrastive (his example is Krongo, not Katcha); stress lengthens consonants (oso ~ osso) and deletes unstressed vowels ('balade ~ 'balde; nefo, pl. na-n'fone). He marks stress on individual words (in the Katcha forms cited it sits on the first root syllable, after any number prefix) but states no rule for where stress falls, so placement is undescribed rather than described as fixed or free.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; notes that stress is 'not equally prominent' across Nuba groups and that in Krongo stress placement distinguishes 'kurugu 'husks' from ku'rugu 'kidneys'. SPA 1979 adds (from the same page) that a High tone may surface as high-falling when stressed before a Low in the same word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (isolated nouns/verbs with Stevenson's pre-syllable stress mark); statement is for the Kadugli-Krongo group as a whole with Katcha (katc1250) as the illustrating dialect, plus Kamdang, Miri and Krongo examples.
new_statements.identity_note: Stevenson's statement is framed for the whole Kadugli-Krongo (Kadu) group and illustrated 'for the most part from KATCHA', i.e. the Katcha/Tolubi dialect (Glottolog katc1250) of Katcha-Kadugli-Miri (katc1249); the same passage cites MIRI (miri1267) and KAMDANG (kamd1238, a Tulishi [tey] dialect) and KRONGO (kron1241) forms, and the one stress-placement minimal pair is Krongo, not Katcha. SPA 1979 files all of it under 'Katcha'. Hall & Hall 2004 treat Kadugli, Katcha and Miri as three of eight Kadugli-Krongo 'languages' with separate orthographies. Sibling audit folders for keig1242, tuli1249, kron1241 and kang1288 hold the same group-level Stevenson/Tucker & Bryan material; is Miriwoong (Australia), unrelated.
